stops.name: The Arrival at Solomon's Jerusalem
stops.campa: The caravan climbs at last into the hill-city of David, and the queen enters Jerusalem with her very great train. The Temple stands new upon its mount; the king's cedar palace, the House of the Forest of Lebanon, gleams. She comes before Solomon and communes with him of all that is in her heart, holding back nothing. She lays out her hard questions one by one, the riddles she carried across a thousand miles of desert, and waits to see whether any thing can be hidden from this king.
stops.quote: And when she was come to Solomon, she communed with him of all that was in her heart.

stops.name: The Riddles Answered
stops.campa: Solomon answers all her questions; there is not any thing hid from the king which he tells her not. In the aggadah she brings sharper snares still: children dressed alike, boys and girls to be told apart; flowers real and artificial that only the bees betray; the water that is neither rain nor spring but the sweat of a labored horse. Each riddle he unknots. The queen who came to prove him is proven; the fame that crossed the desert falls short of the man before her. Her spirit fails within her.
stops.quote: And Solomon told her all her questions: there was not any thing hid from the king, which he told her not.

stops.name: The Glass Floor of the Throne-Court
stops.campa: Solomon has her led into a pavilion whose floor is a smooth expanse of crystal, water gleaming beneath it. 'Enter the palace,' he says. Taking it for a pool, she bares her legs to wade, and the king sees. 'It is a palace whose floor is made smooth with glass,' he tells her. In the aggadah he speaks of the hair upon her legs: beautiful in a man, unseemly in a woman, and the jinn are set to make her a depilatory. The trick that shames her is the trick that turns her: the marvel is real, and so is the God who taught the king to make it.
stops.quote: It was said to her, 'Enter the palace.' But when she saw it, she thought it was a body of water and uncovered her shins. He said, 'Indeed, it is a palace whose floor is made smooth with glass.'

stops.name: 'The Half Was Not Told Me'
stops.campa: She has seen it all: the wisdom, the house he built, the food of his table, the sitting of his servants, the ascent by which he goes up to the House of the LORD, and there is no more spirit in her. She confesses that the report she heard in her own land was a true report, and yet she believed not until she came and her own eyes had seen. The reality outruns every rumor. She blesses the LORD his God, who set him on the throne of Israel to do judgment and justice.
stops.quote: Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the half was not told me: thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard.

stops.name: The Queen Submits to the God of Israel
stops.campa: The sun-worshipper turns. In the Quran she says at the crystal floor: 'My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds.' In the Kebra Nagast she declares it plainly to the king: from this hour she will not worship the sun but the Creator of the sun, the God of Israel. Two scriptures, one conversion: the queen who came bearing incense for the host of heaven kneels now to the One who made the heaven. The gifts are exchanged; the meeting has done its work.
stops.quote: My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

stops.name: The Oath and the Salted Feast
stops.campa: On the eve of her departure, the Kebra Nagast tells, Solomon prepares a feast heavy with spices and salt, and bids the queen sleep in his chamber. She fears him; he swears an oath: 'I will not take thee by force, but swear thou wilt take nothing by force that is in my house.' She swears it, lightly, a queen who wants for nothing. The lamps are lowered. He has set, near her bed, a single bowl of water where the fire's heat will find it in the deep of the salted night.
stops.quote: I will swear to thee that I will not take thee by force, but thou must swear to me that thou wilt not take by force anything that is in my house.

stops.name: The Water Taken, the Oath Broken
stops.campa: In the dark she wakes parched, her throat burning from the salt. She rises and lifts the bowl to drink. At once the king's hand closes on hers. 'Why hast thou broken thine oath, that thou wouldst take nothing by force that is in my house?' Water, he says, is the freest and best of all things, and she has taken it. Released from her word, she is his; that night the queen conceives. He gives her a ring: a token, that any son she bears may one day come and be known to his father by it.
stops.quote: Why hast thou broken the oath that thou hast sworn that thou wouldst not take by force anything that is in my house?

stops.name: The Wooden Bridge, the Sibyl and the Cross
stops.campa: In the medieval legend of the True Cross the queen becomes a Sibyl, a seer. Coming to a stream she finds a beam laid down for a bridge: timber Solomon felled from the holy tree grown on Adam's grave, wood that would serve for nothing else. She will not set foot upon it. She kneels in the dust and adores it, for in a flash she sees the Savior of the world who will one day hang upon that very wood. She tells the king: his glory shall be undone by One crucified upon this beam.

stops.name: The Return South with Solomon's Gifts
stops.campa: Solomon gives to the queen of his royal bounty, all her desire, whatsoever she asks, beside that which he gives of his own hand. Laden now with the wisdom and wealth of Israel, she turns her camels home down the same incense road, past Petra's rose ravines, toward the sea and the southern kingdoms. She carries more than gifts: a ring, an oath broken, and a child quickening in her. The desert that bore her north bears her home again, a different queen than the one who came.
stops.quote: And king Solomon gave unto the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatsoever she asked, beside that which Solomon gave her of his royal bounty. So she turned and went to her own country, she and her servants.

stops.name: The Birth of Menelik on the Road
stops.campa: On the long way home, in the borderlands of her own country, the queen is delivered of a son. She names him Baynā-Leḥkem, whom the ages will call Menelik: the child of the wise king. She raises him in her highland realm as a prince of the God of Israel, and he grows tall and kingly, the very image of Solomon. Always he asks after his father; and his mother keeps the ring against the day he is old enough to cross the desert and stand before the throne in Jerusalem.

stops.name: Aksum, the Queen's Highland Throne Regained
stops.campa: The caravan climbs at last into the stone highlands of Aksum, home. The queen resumes her throne, and it is here, in the Kebra Nagast's telling, that she rules as Makeda, mother of a dynasty not yet born. She has changed the faith of her people: the sun is dethroned, the God of Israel enthroned. The boy Menelik grows to manhood in this city of stelae, hearing always of the far Jerusalem where a king who is his father sits in glory, and of the House of God upon its mountain.
stops.quote: And the Queen departed and came into the country of Bâlâ Zadîsârĕyâ nine months and five days after she had separated from King Solomon.

stops.name: Menelik's Journey to Jerusalem by Way of Gaza
stops.campa: Grown to two-and-twenty, Menelik crosses the deserts his mother crossed, coming up to Jerusalem by way of Gaza. He carries the ring. Men marvel at the road, for his face is Solomon's face; some cry that the king walks among them, though the king sits in his palace. Brought before the throne, the young man draws out the token. Solomon knows it and knows him, and embraces the son of the queen of the south, anoints him king, and names him David after his grandfather, king of the land of Ethiopia.
